title: Fructose or glucose: what pooled trials found for an inflammation marker [fru_glu_ns]
teaser: Researchers have suggested fructose may fan inflammation more than other sugars. [hypothesis] A review pooled trials that gave people fructose or the same calories of glucose. [six_matched] CRP, a blood marker of inflammation, showed no clear difference. [fru_glu_ns] The certainty is low. [grade_fru_glu]
hook: The liver has to handle fructose, and some of it can become fat. [fructose_liver, no_brake] Yet pooled trials found no clear difference in CRP, a blood marker of inflammation, between fructose and glucose. [fru_glu_ns]
populationPanel: Who was tested: 1141 people aged 11 to 72, across 13 controlled trials. [total_1141, ages, studies_13] They were healthy, overweight or obese, with or without diseases in which inflammation is not a main feature. [inclusion_people] The fructose-against-glucose result pooled 6 trials with 403 people. [fru_glu_n] The review left out people with major inflammatory diseases, such as arthritis. [excluded_inflammatory] Trials lasted 2 weeks to 3 months. [durations]

paragraphs: Picture two fuels that look alike. [-] Any cell in the body can burn glucose. [fructose_liver] Fructose has to go to the liver first. [fructose_liver]

In the liver, nothing caps how much fructose comes in. [no_brake] Some of it becomes a building block for fat. [no_brake] Researchers call this making of new fat de novo lipogenesis. [liver_fat_making]

The theory goes one step further. [-] By-products of that new fat may set off inflammation, the body's alarm response. [lipotoxicity] One sign of it is CRP, a blood protein used as a marker of inflammation. [crp_protein]

So the review asked a sharp question. [-] Does fructose raise CRP more than the same calories of glucose? [six_matched] Pooled across trials, the answer was no clear difference. [fru_glu_ns] High-fructose corn syrup against table sugar showed no clear difference either. [hfcs_suc_ns]

The authors offer two reasons a gap may not show. [-] Fructose barely spikes blood sugar, which may spare it some inflammation. [low_gi] And very large sugar doses may inflame through sheer calories, hiding any difference between sugars. [overload]
What the pooled trials tested: fructose against the same calories of glucose. [six_matched] Fructose doses ran from 17 to 217 g a day, for 2 weeks to 3 months. [fructose_doses, durations]
The review gives no advice on how much sugar to eat. [-] The limit the authors cite is the WHO's: at most 10% of daily energy from free sugars. [who_limit] This review did not test that limit. [-]

audit.effect: CRP, fructose against glucose: a pooled difference of −0.03 mg/L (p = 0.90), from 6 trials and 403 people. [md_fru_glu, fru_glu_p, fru_glu_n]
audit.weakEnd: The 95% range runs from −0.52 to 0.46 mg/L. [md_fru_glu] So the true difference could sit on either side of zero. [md_fru_glu] The certainty is low: more trials will likely change the estimate. [grade_fru_glu, grade_meaning]
limitations: Only CRP had enough trials to pool, and some comparisons had few trials. [limit_crp_only, limit_heterogeneity]
Trials lasted two weeks to three months, so they say nothing about years of eating. [limit_duration, limit_years]
The two largest trials did not say how they randomized, lost about a quarter of people, and had industry ties. [limit_two_largest, limit_industry]
Very large doses may hide differences between sugars. [limit_big_doses]
audit.missed: The review took in controlled trials, not only randomized ones. [controlled_trials] Most trials did not account for weight change, a possible link between sugar and inflammation. [limit_weight, weight_mediator]
more: Corn syrup against table sugar: 0.21 mg/L (range −0.11 to 0.53, p = 0.19), 3 trials, 677 people, certainty low. [md_hfcs_suc, hfcs_suc_p, hfcs_suc_n, grade_hfcs_suc]
Inconsistency between trials: 44% and 0%; above 50% counts as substantial. [fru_glu_i2, hfcs_suc_i2, i2_meaning]
Of the six matched trials, two reported a difference on one marker each; the overall picture was inconsistent. [two_of_six, inconsistent]
IL-6, MCP-1 and the other markers had too few trials to pool; no trial reported IL-18 or IL-1RA. [others_not_pooled, no_il18]
Studies that only watched people link sugary drinks with CRP; the authors cannot say if their result agrees. [observational_ssb, cannot_compare]
Funded by German ministries. [funding] One author sits on an ILSI Europe expert group and a carbohydrate consortium. [coi_buyken]

figure.caption: Each band is the 95% range of a pooled difference in CRP. [md_fru_glu, md_hfcs_suc] Both cross the line for no difference. [fru_glu_ns, hfcs_suc_ns]
figure.alt: Two rows. [-] Fructose against glucose: −0.03 mg/L, range −0.52 to 0.46. [md_fru_glu] Corn syrup against table sugar: 0.21 mg/L, range −0.11 to 0.53. [md_hfcs_suc] Both ranges cross zero, the line for no difference. [md_zero]

takeaways: Pooled trials found no clear difference in CRP between fructose and the same calories of glucose. [fru_glu_ns, six_matched]
Table sugar in the trials ran from 50 to 203 g a day. [sucrose_doses] The review compared one sugar with another, so it says nothing about eating less sugar. [-]
Certainty is low, and the review could pool only CRP. [grade_fru_glu, limit_crp_only]
